shared-pool.approach: Treat each array index as a node. The two live lists and the free chain share the same next array; every slot must belong to exactly one chain. Search first, then change links only when the operation can succeed.

steps.text: Initialise one free chain through all slots. Both live heads are -1 because neither list contains values yet.
Track both the current node and its predecessor. Stop at the insertion point; reject a duplicate or full pool before consuming a slot.
Remove one slot from the free chain and link it before current. Update the list head when there is no predecessor; otherwise update the predecessor’s next link.
Find and unlink the target, then put its slot at the front of the free chain. Recycling makes that capacity available to either list.
Follow links, not physical array order. The returned list is only an output copy; it is not the structure’s storage.

shared-pool.trace: Pool(2): free is 0 → 1 → -1. insert(0, 7) gives list 0 slot 0, leaving free=1. insert(1, 9) uses slot 1, leaving free=-1. delete(0, 7) returns slot 0 to free. insert(1, 8) reuses slot 0 before slot 1: list 1 now contains [8, 9].
mistakes: Changing next[current] before unlinking the node can lose the rest of its live list.
Allocating before checking duplicates can leak a free slot.
A duplicate is forbidden within one list; the same value is allowed in the other list.
shared-pool.complexity: For a selected list of n nodes, insert and delete take O(n) in the worst case; relinking a known node takes O(1). values takes O(n). Extra space context: storage is O(capacity); values creates an O(n) output list.

recursive-trace.approach: Each call computes the sum from its index to the end. Record entry before checking the base case; record return only after the smaller suffix has finished. This separates the descent from the return journey.

steps.text: Keep one shared event list. Record enter as soon as visit(i) begins, including the call beyond the final value.
The empty suffix has sum 0. This base case stops recursion without indexing past the list.
Wait for visit(i + 1), then add values[i]. The current call cannot record its final total until the deeper call returns.
Record the completed suffix sum and return that number to the waiting caller.
Start at index 0. Return the event list to the test, rather than the sum computed by visit.

recursive-trace.trace: For [4, 2], entries are enter 0, enter 1, enter 2. The base call returns 0 at index 2; index 1 returns 2 + 0 = 2; index 0 returns 4 + 2 = 6. Return events therefore appear in reverse index order: ["return", 2, 0], ["return", 1, 2], ["return", 0, 6].
mistakes: Checking the base case before logging enter omits the final entry event.
Logging return before the recursive call gives the wrong event order.
Returning events from visit breaks addition: visit must return a number.
recursive-trace.complexity: For n values there are n + 1 calls, each doing constant work: O(n) time. Extra space context: the call stack and event list both grow to O(n).

register-import.approach: Parse with csv.reader, reject invalid rows before writing, and insert accepted rows inside one transaction. Expected bad input is skipped; an unexpected database failure escapes the transaction and rolls back the whole batch.

steps.text: Open as UTF-8 with CSV newline handling. Check the exact header before any insert; csv.reader preserves commas inside quoted names.
Use the connection’s transaction context for the batch. Count rows from 2 because the header occupied line 1; reject the wrong field count before unpacking.
Use short-circuit validation: establish ASCII decimal text before calling int. Reject missing names, non-positive IDs and scores outside 0–100.
Check the database before each insert. This detects both pre-existing IDs and accepted IDs earlier in the same batch, preserving the first valid record.

Bind values through placeholders, increment the accepted count, then return counts after successful transaction exit. A database error propagates instead of returning a misleading partial-success result.

register-import.trace: With an empty database: line 2 is 1,Ari,90 → insert ID 1; line 3 is 1,Mei,80 → reject duplicate; line 4 is 2,Kai,101 → reject range. Return [1, [3, 4]]. Separately, if a later valid row triggers a database error, the earlier ID 1 insert must also be rolled back.
mistakes: Splitting text on commas corrupts quoted names such as "Ari, Tan".
Catching every database error and continuing can commit a partial import.
Interpolating names into SQL mishandles quotes; use placeholders.
register-import.complexity: CSV scanning takes O(n) for n rows. Database lookups and inserts add work; indexed operations are typically logarithmic in table size, so avoid claiming the entire import is always O(n). Extra space context: rows are streamed, but rejected line numbers can grow to O(n).
